Not that I am necessarily in agreement with the other dude, but if I may offer an alternative viewpoint to this whole 'abortion' issue?

When I see the Pro-Life/Choice debate, I see one major issue that both sides seem to ignore...namely the question of "Does a government that respects personal autonomy over oneself, such as the United States, have any right to force one human being to use their body, for any length of time, to support the life of another?" Well, let's examine this further...

Theoretical Scenario: Person A has been found to be capable of providing viable biomatter to Patient B, in a lifesaving medical procedure that will ensure Patient B has the capability to go on to live a full, productive life. Person A, however, does not want to undergo the procedure. Patient B has petitioned the government to step in on their behalf to compel Person A to provide said biomatter, without which Patient B shall perish unquestionably. Person A is the sole eligible donor to provide said biomatter for the procedure. If this case were to come before a court of law, whose argument would the law support the most?

Fortunately, we already have established Case Law to decide this argument for us, but just for the argument's sake, let's examine the merits of each argument:

  • Person A's argument is that they, as a functional and autonomous human being, have the right to say what procedures they undergo, and what their bodies are used to support, whether that be through organ transplant, biomatter donation, or other means, and that for the State to compel them, against their will, to provide said biomatter for Patient B would violate that personal autonomy and infringe on their rights, as such.

  • The State, representing Patient B, claims that Patient B has a right to live their life, and that if they have to infringe on Person A's rights of personal autonomy to ensure that, then they view that as a decent trade-off to ensure that Patient B has a right to live their life.

Person A certainly raises a good point, in that they have the right to personal autonomy, and that the government is constitutionally bound to respect that. Medical personnel must go through extensive red tape documenting Person A's consent for any medical procedure, whatsoever, to ensure that any process they go through is undergone with full recognition and consent. As Person A is not, at any time, on record as consenting to allowing Patient B to using their personal biomatter to survive, we must assume that such consent has not been given. As such, until such consent is given, and is ongoing for the full time necessary for such procedure to be successful, the State is compelled to recognize Person A's right to personal autonomy; even if Person A's position is morally indefensible, their right to personal autonomy outweighs any interest Patient B may have in requiring acquisition of Person A's biomatter. Just as a person walking down the street is not legally required to keep the beggar from freezing, though we may consider him morally bankrupt if he is fully capable of doing so and instead chooses to do nothing, we cannot legally compel him to do so, even if it is to mean the beggar's death.

Similarly, if we are to grant the personhood argument for a blastocyst, and we assume that said clump of cells is human, we still have the dilemma of compelling another human to use their body to support the life of another, without that person's consent, coerced by the State. To quote the precedent-establishing case McFall v Shimp, :

For a society which respects the rights of one individual, to sink its teeth into the jugular vein or neck of one of its members and suck from it sustenance for another member, is revolting to our hard-wrought concepts of jurisprudence.

In this vein, I believe that a conservative case can be made for the Pro-Choice position, even if one finds the position personally distasteful and morally abhorrent. If one is truly concerned about the intrusion of government into personal affairs, I believe one would do much better pursuing those ideals by ensuring mechanisms exist so that abortions are less necessary (Such as a policy trade-off by ensuring easier access to contraceptive devices at local health departments, to provide one example) rather than promoting government intrusion into the Doctor-Client relationship, and mandating that a woman must, by government decree, surrender her bodily autonomy to support another human being for ~9 months.

We don't allow such a blatant violation of bodily autonomy by the State in cases of Bone Marrow, so why should we allow for such, just because the specific body part being used is different? The principle still stands, regardless. One could say that the Christian faith finds abortion to be abhorrent, but then we've stepped into the question of Church Doctrine versus Government, in violation of the 1st Amendment...and doctrine aside, that is in spite of the Conservative values of small government, not due to it.

In short, just because I support a woman's right to terminate a pregnancy, doesn't mean I like her doing so. I support the right of skinheads to say racist shit, even if I find what they have to say distasteful...because the moment I advocate using the State to coerce them into silence, I sign the warrant for my own censorship. If one is to say it is okay for the State to compel another human to use one's body to support the life of another, they sign their own warrant for the State to compel them to surrender, in principle, any portion, or whole thereof, to support the life of another individual.

The right to bodily autonomy, as such, demands the right to terminate unwanted pregnancies. However, that also means that the right to personal property means that I don't have to pay for them, and they can be responsible for funding their own procedures.

Let the women get their abortions, and the women can keep their hands (And the hands of the State, taking money by proxy, through taxation) out of our wallets.

I've heard the gist of this argument before, but never so well articulated. Bravo. I am curious, however, about one thing regarding your last two sentences. Do you believe society, on average, is better served with or without what amount to unwanted children? I, for one, will gladly pay a few dollars a year if it means I (the State) don't have to deal with the likely impacts to society of an unwanted child brought to term for no other reason than the mother doesn't have "easy access" to an abortion.

The pragmatic side of me agrees that society would be better served without, as you phrased it, 'unwanted children'. However, I see this problem as a multi-tiered one, with many contributing factors, none of which will be solved merely by making easy access to abortion available. Take, for example, the issue of poverty-level mothers. With welfare, we already incentivize single-mother homes, because the State looks to the Father to provide for these things, and when he isn't there, the State steps in to assist. Further more, with the advent of No-Fault divorce, but keeping the old, once-decried-as-patriarchal norms of the expectation of men to still provide for their ex-wives (Thus giving women the benefits of a clean break with none of the attendant responsibilities, as a "clean break" would imply she then rejoin the workforce instead of sponging off of her ex), we have removed any potential negative consequences for women to break up the Central Family Unit.

This is literally lethal discrimination, all for some feel-good, White Knight aspect of "Think of the Women..." Politics is about compromise, and while idealogues are useful for Party elders, the media, and newspapers, they tend to bode poorly for the policymaking chambers of State, so I'm at least willing to listen, even if it rubs my political sense the wrong way. But the way things currently are, with women receiving the vast majority of public funding while paying a pittance in taxes to support all that public spending, I could not, in good faith, support such a measure outside of specific multi-tiered/multi-party-beneficiary reform efforts such as Legal Paternal Surrender (Basically what they call "Male Abortion".
